name: Buk u vodojemu

location.address: Březinova ulice, near the water reservoir, Frýdlant

story:
Frýdlant protected this beech by drawing a circle around it. Ten metres in every direction from the trunk, in force since 10 March 2005, and inside that circle the tree is left alone.

What stands in the middle of it is a copper beech 27 metres tall with a trunk 4.22 metres round, on Březinova street beside the town water reservoir, a few minutes from the railway station. Coming up the street you have the Glück Villa below to the south and the hospital across to the east, with the Řasnice river running behind. This is a town tree in the plainest sense, on a working street rather than in a park, and it is by a wide margin the largest thing on that street.

A purple beech is not something a wood produces by itself. The dark form is a garden cultivar, propagated by hand and planted deliberately, which means somebody chose this spot and put it here on purpose. Who, and when, is not recorded anywhere we can find.

So the register gives the height and the girth and stops, which leaves the trunk as the only clock the tree has. Nobody has published an age. If you know when it went in, or whose garden it once stood in, tell us and we will add it.
access: Free, on a public street beside the town's water reservoir
transport: Central Frýdlant, short walk from the town centre and railway station

name: Hraniční buk (Cínovec border beech)

location.address: Roadside at the Cínovec-Zinnwald border crossing site (Dubí, Teplice District), marked with an information plaque

story:
The tree standing here is not the tree the stories are about. The original border beech was reputedly planted in 1537 on the line between Bohemia and Saxony and grew to some six metres round. It began failing after 1945, was down to a single living branch by the 1960s, and lightning finished it in the 1970s. What grows here now went into the same ground on 18 August 2007, with an information plaque beside it. It is a young tree, slim and easy to walk past, standing in the exact spot where a mountain road has crossed a border for centuries.

The old beech collected the traffic. Emperor Joseph II is recorded passing it in 1766 and again in 1779. Goethe came through in 1813. Napoleon is supposed to have rested under it, which is the sort of thing said about every large tree on a route an army once used, and is worth about what it costs to repeat. All of that belongs to the site and to the tree that is gone, not to the sapling.

So this is a young beech holding an old address at the Cínovec crossing to Zinnwald, up in the Ore Mountains. Come for the place and the plaque that explains it. Come back in a century for the tree.
access: Free, roadside historic site at a mountain border crossing
transport: Cínovec, on the Czech-German border near Dubí, Teplice District

name: Buk lesní v Proseči pod Ještědem

location.address: Hlubocký ridge above the hamlet of Padouchov, beside the disused limestone quarry over which the Ještěd waterfall (Ještědský vodopád) falls, Proseč pod Ještědem
location.neighbourhood: Padouchov, Proseč pod Ještědem, Liberec Region

story:
There is a waterfall here that nobody designed. Eight metres of water drops over the cut wall of a limestone quarry that stopped working and filled back in with forest, and the beech stands right beside it, five metres round at the trunk, with heavy root buttresses flaring out of the ground all round the base.

It is a protected memorial tree on the Hlubocký ridge above the hamlet of Padouchov, reached on foot on the trail up to the Ještěd waterfall from Proseč pod Ještědem. The quarry underneath is now a protected bat roost, so this small piece of ground has been left alone twice over: once by the quarrymen who walked away from it, and once by law.

Nobody has recorded an age or a height. The municipality publishes the girth, five metres, and nothing else. For a beech that is well into old age without saying how far into it, and there is no plaque or local account to settle the question. If you know more, tell us.

One thing to know before you go. Our pin marks the waterfall and quarry area rather than a coordinate anybody has stood on and checked, so it is close rather than exact, and you will have to look around a little once you are up there.
access: Free, reached on foot via the hiking trail to the Ještěd waterfall
transport: Hamlet of Padouchov, near Světlá pod Ještědem, Liberec Region; reached on foot from local trails

name: Pastýřský buk (Shepherd's Beech)

location.address: Northern edge of the Lazy settlement, on the edge of a pasture, Slavkovský les
location.neighbourhood: Lazy, Cheb District, Karlovy Vary Region

story:
Half of this beech is lying on the ground, and both halves are still legally protected. The standing part leans, held together with flexible bindings since the spring of 2015. The fallen part has been left where it came down.

It has been going wrong slowly. Heavy icing broke its strongest limb at the end of 2014. Some years later a whole side went over, helped along by Kretzschmaria deusta, a wood decay fungus that blackens a trunk until the tree looks as though it has been through a fire. Sources give the height as 22 metres or as 17, and the lower figure is almost certainly the tree as it is now. The trunk is 5.88 metres round and the crown once spread 21 metres across, which is what a beech does when it grows up alone with nothing to compete with. Nobody has dated it precisely; the estimates run from about 200 to 280 years.

That is where it stands, at 807 metres on the edge of the Lazy settlement in the Slavkovský les, out on open grazing land. In the autumn of 2003 it came second in the national Tree of the Year vote.

Local story has it growing from a shepherd's staff pushed into the ground during a storm, which sprouted overnight. Nobody claims to have watched.

best_time.label: October, when the last standing half turns copper on an open hillside

access: Free, standing alone on open pastureland at 807m elevation, reachable on foot
transport: Hamlet of Lazy, Cheb District; rural, reached on foot/by road, no public transport at the tree itself

name: Buk v Podlesí

location.neighbourhood: Mcely, Nymburk District, Central Bohemian Region

story:
This beech has been under legal protection since 25 July 1978, which is longer than almost anything else on this map, and that is very close to everything anybody has written down about it.

The rest of the record is two numbers. Twenty-six metres tall, 4.15 metres round at the trunk. It stands in the Podlesí woods near the village of Mcely in the Nymburk district of Central Bohemia, in forest rather than in a park or a churchyard, which is where protected trees usually turn up. The state register carries the entry and the coordinate. Mcely's own page about its memorial trees names other trees and not this one. No age has ever been recorded and no local story attaches to it.

That absence is worth something. Most protected trees are protected because a town decided it loved them, and the loving leaves a paper trail of competitions, plaques and newspaper pieces. This one was singled out nearly fifty years ago by somebody doing an inventory, and then left standing in a wood, and it has been quietly getting on with it ever since.

Which does mean the age is anybody's guess, and we would rather not guess. If you know roughly how old it is, or why it was designated, tell us and we will put it on the page.
access: Free, standing in a forest near the village of Mcely
transport: Village of Mcely, Nymburk District; rural, reached on foot/by road

name: Buk u kostela v Jihlavě (Beech by St James's Church)

location.address: Beside the Church of St James the Greater (kostel sv. Jakuba), on the grounds of a former medieval cemetery, Jihlava

story:
A group of Jihlava students campaigned this beech to the national Tree of the Year title in the autumn of 2003. Twenty-three years later it is entered again, in a competition for the tree of the quarter century, still standing beside the church of St James the Greater in the middle of town.

It is a copper beech, 4.44 metres round, 19 metres tall, with a crown 21.4 metres across, and nobody agrees how old it is. An estimate made in 1994, four years after it was declared a memorial tree, put it at 211 years. Another in 2003 put it at 132. The two readings are of the same trunk, nine years apart, and they differ by almost a century, so take the range and not either end of it.

What is not in doubt is the ground it grows out of. A cemetery surrounded this church from the early Middle Ages until the burials moved elsewhere, and the open space around the beech is what was left when they went. However old it turns out to be, it has spent its whole life rooted in a graveyard.

It stands in an open public churchyard in central Jihlava, a short walk from the main square, free and reachable at any hour.
access: Free, in a public churchyard/square in central Jihlava
transport: Central Jihlava, short walk from the main square

name: Lukavický dub (Dub na Hrádku / Dub u Lukavické tvrze)

location.address: On the open ground of a former fortress (Hrádek), Lukavice

story:
Somebody once tried to kill this oak with a shovel. Before the First World War the management of the Auersberg estate had dozens of cartloads of soil stripped away from around its roots, which is a slow and deniable way to finish a tree. It is still standing, and in 2024 the country voted it Czech Tree of the Year.

It grows on the open ground of the Hrádek at Lukavice, the site of a fortress belonging to the local nobility, and it stood in that courtyard while the courtyard was still a courtyard. The trunk is more than seven metres round and the tree is 31 metres tall. Its age is estimated at nearly 800 years, which would put its first seasons somewhere in the thirteenth century; that is an estimate rather than a count, and the honest band around it is wide.

Eight centuries of standing still has turned it into a habitat rather than a tree. It carries its own fungi, beetles and bats, most of which need wood that has been dead for a long time inside a tree that is still alive. It has been legally protected since 1990.

The sources call it dub, oak, and go no further. If you can tell a pedunculate from a sessile by the acorn stalks, tell us which this is.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the whole frame of it is readable

access: Free, on open community ground at the former fortress site
